steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper introducing a game-based benchmark that evaluates large language models as intelligent agents. Explain why LLM agents need such a benchmark, why games are a good fit, and briefly describe the benchmark.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Creating intelligent agents, which perceive their environment and take autonomous actions, has been one of the core objectives of A.I. Recently large language models (LLMs) made remarkable progress on various tasks. Some language models show exceptional planning, reasoning, and problem-solving abilities, and this gives them potential as generalist agents for virtual-reality or for real-world problem-solving.

This potential attracted strong interest in applications where LLM systems actively call tools and APIs to complete a wide range of task goals, and where they actively interact with an environment and make changes in it to achieve specific results. LLMs as agents could be seen as an important step toward next-gen automation.

There is a lot of public attention, but the capabilities of LLMs as agents have not been studied systematically, partly because there is no standardized LLM benchmark for agent-environment interaction. Current LLM benchmarks were designed for static knowledge and reasoning, or for helpful and harmless conversations, and they overlook applications to intelligent agents.

There are 4 key challenges for intelligent LLM agents that previous benchmarks do not capture. First, a lot of real-world tasks need the agent to do long-horizon planning. Second, many events are probabilistic and an intelligent agent should understand the odds. Third, an intelligent agent needs spatial reasoning to understand our 3D world. Fourth, an intelligent agent should be able to learn from interactions or mistakes when it encounters unseen situations.

Games, on the other hand, have long been seen as go-to benchmarks for intelligent generalist agents. At the core of game design, successful games often involve “problem-solving”, “calculation of odds”, “spatial reasoning”, “changing difficulties”, and “well-defined and quantifiable outcome”, so they are a perfect complement to existing LLM benchmarks. Also, some game environments are procedurally generated and the game states grow exponentially, and this makes games more robust against evaluation dataset contamination, which was observed in recent works. In our experiments we see that LLMs struggle to memoize intermediate states of a simple 3-disk Tower of Hanoi game.

We take a unique agent perspective for benchmarking LLMs and introduce SmartPlay, a benchmark made from 6 distinct games that are augmented with language descriptors for the visual observation (Figure 1). It offers up to 20 different settings and infinite environment variations. Each game has unique challenges that span multiple dimensions of intelligent agents, as detailed in Table 3. The games have different complexity, from simple one-step reasoning and rule-following in Bandits, to intricate long-term planning, multi-hop dependencies, and learning from interactions in Crafter and Hanoi. SmartPlay puts LLM agents in both deterministic and stochastic settings, and it demands skills from basic text understanding to 3D spatial reasoning.

The games in SmartPlay were built with well-defined objectives and evaluation metrics: completion rate, reward, score. So SmartPlay provides a fully automated pipeline for standardized evaluation of LLMs. We use SmartPlay to compare how recent LLMs perform as agents, and we identify several research gaps for applying LLMs as agents. We believe SmartPlay sets a goal that can be reached in a short time-frame but is formidable enough to require new breakthroughs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Creating intelligent agents [4] that perceive their environment and perform autonomous actions has been one of the core objectives of A.I. [5,6] Recently, large language models (LLMs) [7,8,9,10,11,12] have made remarkable progress in various tasks [13]. Some language models demonstrate exceptional planning [14,15], reasoning [16,17], and problem-solving [18,19] abilities, giving them potential as generalist agents for virtual-reality [20] or real-world problem-solving.

Such potential has attracted strong interest in applications where LLM systems actively invoke tools and APIs to complete a wide range of task goals [21,22,23,24,25], and actively interact with and make changes in an environment to achieve specific results [26,24,15,27]. LLMs as agents could be seen as an important step toward next-gen automation.

Despite great public attention, the capabilities of LLMs as agents have not been systematically studied, partly due to the lack of a standardized LLM benchmark for agent-environment interaction. Current LLM benchmarks have been designed for static knowledge and reasoning [28,29,30,31], or helpful and harmless conversations [32,33,34], overlooking applications to intelligent agents.

We note 4 key challenges for intelligent LLM agents that previous benchmarks do not capture. First, many real-world tasks require an agent to do long-horizon planning. Second, many events are probabilistic and an intelligent agent is expected to understand the odds. Third, an intelligent agent needs spatial reasoning to understand our 3D world. Fourth, when it encounters unseen situations, an intelligent agent should be able to learn from interactions or mistakes.

On the other hand, games have long been identified as go-to benchmarks for intelligent generalist agents [35,36,37,38,39,40,2,41,3]. At the core of game design [42], successful games often involve “problem-solving”, “calculation of odds”, “spatial reasoning”, “changing difficulties”, and “well-defined and quantifiable outcome”, thereby offering a perfect complement to existing LLM benchmarks. Finally, some game environments are procedurally generated and their game states grow exponentially, making games more robust against the evaluation dataset contamination observed in recent works [12]. Experimentally, we observe that LLMs struggle to memoize intermediate states of a simple 3-disk Tower of Hanoi game.

Taking a unique agent perspective in benchmarking LLMs, we introduce SmartPlay, a benchmark from 6 distinct games augmented with language descriptors for visual observation (Figure 1), offering up to 20 different settings and infinite environment variations. Each game presents unique challenges that span multiple dimensions of intelligent agents, as detailed in Table 3. The games range in complexity, from simple one-step reasoning and rule-following in Bandits, to intricate long-term planning, multi-hop dependencies, and learning from interactions in Crafter [2] and Hanoi. SmartPlay engages LLM agents in both deterministic and stochastic settings, demanding skills from basic text understanding to 3D spatial reasoning.

Games in SmartPlay have been built with well-defined objectives and evaluation metrics: completion rate, reward, score. Therefore, SmartPlay provides a fully automated pipeline for standardized evaluation of LLMs. We use SmartPlay to compare the agent performance of recent LLMs, and we identify several research gaps for applying LLMs as agents. We believe that SmartPlay sets a goal that is reachable in a short time-frame yet formidable enough to require new breakthroughs.
